stubs.angle: Asks what the model, the view and the view model each do in a WPF, WinUI or Avalonia app and how they talk to each other.
stubs.answerHinge: The view model exposes state and commands without referencing the view, and the view connects to it only through data binding and commands, which makes the view model testable without a UI.

stubs.angle: A runnable view model prints property names from PropertyChanged; FullName depends on FirstName and LastName, but the setters never report FullName, so the user must find the line where the dependent notification is missing.
stubs.answerHinge: A computed property has no setter of its own, so the setters of the properties it depends on must also raise PropertyChanged for it, otherwise bindings to it never refresh.

stubs.angle: A runnable view model whose setter raises PropertyChanged before it assigns the backing field; the subscriber reads the property in the handler and prints the old value, and the user must find the misordered line.
stubs.answerHinge: Subscribers re-read the property inside the PropertyChanged handler, so the event must be raised after the backing field holds the new value.

stubs.angle: Asks why a WinUI TextBlock with Text="{x:Bind ViewModel.Status}" never shows updates even though the view model raises PropertyChanged.
stubs.answerHinge: The default mode of x:Bind is OneTime, unlike {Binding}, whose default for TextBlock.Text is OneWay, so Mode=OneWay must be set explicitly.

stubs.angle: Asks which property in WPF can be the target of a {Binding} markup extension, with options mixing plain CLR properties of a custom control, INotifyPropertyChanged properties and dependency properties.
stubs.answerHinge: The binding target must be a dependency property of a DependencyObject, while the source can be any CLR property; a binding on a plain CLR property of a control fails.

stubs.angle: Asks what happens at run time when a WPF binding path names a property that the DataContext does not have.
stubs.answerHinge: No exception is thrown: the binding leaves the target at its fallback or default value and only writes a System.Windows.Data error to the debug trace output, which PresentationTraceSources can make more detailed.

stubs.subtopic: WPF binding and the UI thread
stubs.angle: Asks which changes made from a Task.Run thread are safe when the data is bound in WPF: setting a scalar view model property, adding to a bound ObservableCollection, adding after EnableCollectionSynchronization, setting TextBox.Text directly, and adding through Dispatcher.InvokeAsync.
stubs.answerHinge: WPF marshals PropertyChanged of scalar bound properties to the UI thread, but a CollectionChanged from another thread throws NotSupportedException unless BindingOperations.EnableCollectionSynchronization is used or the change is dispatched, and controls themselves are thread-affine.

stubs.angle: Asks which statements about compiled bindings in Avalonia 11 are true, covering x:DataType, build-time path checking, reflection use and behaviour without a declared data type.
stubs.answerHinge: Compiled bindings need the data type declared with x:DataType, resolve paths at build time so a wrong path is a build error, and avoid reflection-based binding at run time.

stubs.angle: Asks how x:Bind differs from {Binding} in WinUI in where it gets its source, when the binding is resolved and what that means for performance and refactoring.
stubs.answerHinge: x:Bind is turned into generated code at compile time and is rooted in the page or control class itself rather than DataContext, so it is type-checked and avoids reflection, but it cannot follow a DataContext set at run time.

stubs.angle: Asks what problem the WPF weak event pattern solves for view models that subscribe to long-lived services and how WeakEventManager changes the reference graph.
stubs.answerHinge: A normal event subscription lets the long-lived source keep the listener alive, while WeakEventManager holds the listener through a weak reference so a closed view and its view model can be collected without an explicit unsubscribe.

stubs.angle: Loading 50,000 search results by calling Add on a bound ObservableCollection in a loop freezes a WPF screen for seconds; how do you diagnose and fix it?
stubs.answerHinge: Each Add raises its own CollectionChanged and makes the bound view update item by item, and WPF collection views reject range notifications, so the fix is to build the items first and swap in one new collection with a single PropertyChanged or raise one Reset.

stubs.angle: Asks how the WPF layout system computes element sizes and positions and what makes a property change trigger a new layout pass for part of the tree.
stubs.answerHinge: Layout is a recursive two-pass process, Measure then Arrange, and properties marked AffectsMeasure or AffectsArrange invalidate the element so the pass reruns up and down from it, which is why frequent size changes in deep trees are expensive.

stubs.angle: Asks how Avalonia puts its controls on screen on Windows, Linux and macOS and why they look the same on every platform.
stubs.answerHinge: Avalonia does not wrap native OS controls; it draws every control itself through its own rendering pipeline, by default with Skia, onto a surface the platform provides.

stubs.angle: Asks why a WPF control property bound OneWay to the view model stops updating after code-behind assigns the property once.
stubs.answerHinge: Setting a local value replaces the OneWay binding expression, so later source changes are lost; SetCurrentValue changes the effective value while keeping the binding.

stubs.angle: Asks how a tech lead chooses between hand-written base classes, CommunityToolkit.Mvvm source generators and a reactive framework for a new desktop product built by a team of eight.
stubs.answerHinge: The choice weighs boilerplate removal and compile-time generated notification code against the learning curve, debuggability and long-term support of the library, and must be fixed as one team convention rather than mixed per screen.

stubs.angle: Two teams add styles to merged ResourceDictionaries in one WPF shell's App.xaml and keep breaking each other's screens; what do you change technically and in the process?
stubs.answerHinge: Resource lookup walks up to application resources and a duplicate key in merged dictionaries resolves to the last merged one, so ownership, key naming rules and module-scoped dictionaries are needed instead of one global pool.

stubs.angle: Asks how a lead introduces MVVM into a large WPF application whose logic lives in code-behind event handlers, without a feature freeze.
stubs.answerHinge: Migrate screen by screen, starting with new and frequently changed screens, extract logic into testable view models behind bindings and commands, and set a rule that new code-behind may only hold view-specific behaviour.

stubs.angle: Management wants a .NET Framework 4.8 WPF line-of-business app moved to .NET 8 this quarter; how do you assess and plan the move?
stubs.answerHinge: WPF on .NET 8 runs only on Windows with a net8.0-windows target, so the risk lies in third-party control suites, unsupported .NET Framework APIs and project-format changes, which call for an inventory and a project-by-project upgrade rather than a big-bang switch.

stubs.angle: Asks how an architect chooses between WPF, WinUI 3 and Avalonia for a line-of-business desktop product that must ship on Windows now, may need Linux and macOS later and will live for ten years.
stubs.answerHinge: WPF and WinUI 3 are Windows-only while Avalonia is cross-platform with self-drawn controls, so the decision hinges on platform reach, ecosystem and vendor maturity against migration cost, and a UI-agnostic view model layer keeps the choice reversible.

stubs.angle: Asks which design decisions keep one view model library reusable across WPF, WinUI and Avalonia front ends.
stubs.answerHinge: View models stay portable when they depend only on BCL contracts such as INotifyPropertyChanged, ICommand and ObservableCollection<T>, reach UI services through injected interfaces, and use no framework types such as Visibility, brushes or Application.Current.Dispatcher.
